title: After raising $1B in funding, Valar Atomics plans to mass produce small nuclear reactors for the AI industry
teaser: From prototype to mass factory: Nuclear startups are raising billions to use small reactors to power AI's skyrocketing data center needs.
summary: Advanced nuclear startups Valar Atomics and Antares Nuclear are vying to solve the unprecedented power demand fueled by the AI revolution. Valar Atomics recently closed a $1 billion funding round, signaling its shift from building prototypes to mass-producing Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) on a factory line. This scalability is crucial because AI data centers require reliable energy sources at an immense scale. Notably, Valar demonstrated its reactor successfully powering an Nvidia Blackwell system, leading to plans for a 30MW nuclear-powered AI facility in Utah. Meanwhile, Antares Nuclear raised $470 million and aims to test SMRs on Air Force bases. The development of these modular reactors promises to revolutionize the energy sector by offering a faster, cheaper alternative to traditional power plants, addressing both cost issues and the urgent need for massive electrification.
author: Mike Wheatley
content: Nuclear energy startup Valar Atomics Inc. said today it has raised a bumper $1 billion Series B funding round to help it move from building prototype small nuclear reactors to manufacturing them at scale on a production line. Today's round was led by Sequoia Capital and saw participation from nine other venture capital firms, including Valor Equity Partners and Conviction. In addition, Valar said it has also secured a separate $200 million credit facility from Erebor, J.P. Morgan, Crescent Cove and Hercules Capital. Valar Atomics founder and Chief Executive Isaiah Taylor said the investment will help the company to change what it does, rather than what it designs. It can now shift from "demonstrating the operability of an integrated reactor system to producing fleets of them en masse," he told Bloomberg in an interview. The startup intends to build hundreds of small modular reactors, known as SMRs, which are basically miniaturized power plants, on production lines, similar to how cars are manufactured. Building them this way will be much faster and cheaper than the traditional way power plants are constructed, it says. In June, Valar Atomics partnered with Nvidia Corp. to demonstrate the effectiveness of its small Ward-250 test reactor, which was installed in a data center and used to power Blackwell graphics processing unit running artificial intelligence workloads. "This marked the first and only time that an advanced reactor has directly powered AI infrastructure, and was the first time in history a startup generated nuclear power," Taylor wrote in a blog post announcing today's round. Following that demonstration, Valar announced an expanded partnership with Nvidia to build a complete 30-megawatt nuclear-powered AI facility in Utah. The reactor's design integrates a closed-loop cooling system that could reduce the facility's water usage from around 2.6 million gallons per megawatt per year to just a few hundred gallons. Taylor told Bloomberg that the startup's SMR development lifecycle is speeding up exponentially, as it implements the lessons learned in building them to improve its processes. "It took two years to complete the NOVA core, then it took seven months to take Ward 250 critical," he said of the company's first two SMRs. "With each reactor built, the tick rate will become smaller until Valar is producing tens, hundreds and then thousands of reactors per year," he added. The idea is that Valar will eventually establish a giant factor that's able to churn out SMRs that can then be delivered directly to data centers, industrial sites and other facilities that need a reliable energy source. The company believes its modular approach can dramatically reduce the costs in a nuclear energy industry that's renowned for budget overruns and project delays. It's an idea that's also being pursued in China and in Russia, where state-backed corporations have already gotten the small power plants up and running . But to date, there are none in service in the U.S. Taylor says the rise of AI and its massive power demands have added a sense of urgency to the company's mission, which is why today's round is such a critical milestone for his company. "AI is building very quickly, and we need a lot of power in every direction," he insisted. "This is really about scale for us, this is the firepower that we need to go and build." It's notable that Valar isn't alone in trying to build fleets of SMRs that can power the AI factories of the future, In fact, it's just one of several U.S. startups pursuing more cost-effective and scalable ways of starting self-sustaining nuclear chain reactions that can generate the continuous energy needed for AI. Rivals including X-energy Reactor Co., which raised $700 million in November before going public in April; Radiant Industries Inc., which raised $300 million in December; Aalo Atomics Inc., which pulled in $100 million in August 2025; and Bluecore Energy Inc., which last month closed on a $10 million seed funding round to pursue its idea of shrinking nuclear reactors and putting them on barges. title: The studio behind Pokémon struggles to find its voice in Beast of Reincarnation
teaser: New Pokémon adventure Beast of Reincarnation shines with unique combat but struggles under the weight of derivative ideas and an underdeveloped plot.
summary: A critical review details 'Beast of Reincarnation,' a sci-fi action RPG set in a postapocalyptic Japan 2,000 years from now. The protagonist, Emma, fights an immortal beast by absorbing powers from mutated monsters. While the combat is thrilling—featuring abilities like growing vines out of her hair for traversal and utilizing a dog companion—the review criticizes the game's narrative depth, describing its pervasive mystery as frustratingly underdeveloped. Furthermore, the article points out that many mechanics and ideas feel derivative of established titles like Dark Souls, Monster Hunter, and Nier: Automata. Despite these issues, it is praised for creating a compelling sense of melancholic moodiness. The game launches on August 4th across PS5, Xbox, and PC.
author: Andrew Webster
content: You have to imagine that the team at Game Freak is bursting with ideas. The studio puts out new mainline Pokémon adventures with a machinelike precision. But every so often it launches a curious experiment, whether it's an action title about a militarized elephant or turning horse races into a card game , showing that it's capable of more than the latest generation of pocket monsters. That's part of what makes the idea of Beast of Reincarnation so enticing. Here is an established studio breaking free of the franchise it has become known for to make its take on a blockbuster action game. Unfortunately new ideas are in short supply in Beast , and aside from its slick action, there's little that hasn't been done before. Beast of Reincarnation takes place exactly 2,000 years in the future in a postapocalyptic vision of Japan that blends sci-fi and magic. Humans still exist, though many of them transferred their consciousness to robotic golems in order to survive the calamity that ruined the world. The real problem is that a mysterious blight has infected the landscape, turning wildlife into vicious, mutated monsters. Even worse: This seems to portend the return of the titular beast, a powerful creature that, as its name implies, appears to be immortal. You play as a wandering mercenary-type named Emma who has the ability to absorb the powers of fallen mutants, and soon she's tasked with traversing the world to power up so that she can take down the beast for good. It's not a bad setup for an action game, as it gives you a reason to keep moving forward. Emma is constantly on the hunt for the next big creature that she can use to get stronger before taking on her final task. Beast of Reincarnation isn't an open-world game, but instead is divided into a series of big locations that you travel between as the story progresses. The standout feature of the game is its action. Emma is a speedy samurai type, wielding a blade and various bows. At first, Beast seems like Dark Souls or Elden Ring , a game built around dodging and parrying, with little room for error. But as you unlock new powers, it proves to be something a little different. Emma's signature ability is that vines and plants can grow out of her hair. This sounds weird, but it's also incredibly useful; she can build bridges to traverse big gaps, or use her hair like a grappling hook to reach locations up high. She also has an adorable and gigantic magical dog companion who follows her everywhere and provides a hand with combat and tedious chores like collecting loot. Emma's powers are especially helpful in battle. Slowly she gains abilities that let her zip around the battlefield, using her hair to quickly gain ground on an enemy, deliver an attack from above, or team up with her powerful pup for a devastating blow. Her hair can even improve your stealth: At one point I unlocked a skill that caused tall plants to sprout wherever I crouched, temporarily giving me some cover before delivering a silent kill. It takes a few hours for things to open up, but eventually Beast 's combat has plenty of room for freedom and creativity. The same can't be said for the rest of the experience. Initially, Beast 's postapocalyptic world is compelling because it's full of mystery. You know almost nothing about the history of the world, but there are hints of interesting dynamics, like the human-infused machines and how they evolved differently from flesh-and-blood people. But Beast pushes the idea of mystery to a frustrating extreme. Everything in this game is mysterious: the landscape, Emma herself, her two human travel companions, her giant dog, the little girl that only Emma can see, the other wandering fighters she encounters in the world. I love a story that is full of secrets and intrigue, but I barely understood what I was even doing in Beast until at least a dozen hours into the game. It doesn't help that the game hides explanations of many of its key elements in a tutorial menu. And when you do finally get answers to the big mysteries, they're mostly underwhelming. The story isn't the only place that feels underdeveloped or uninspired. There are a number of gameplay elements - like the ability to grow your own food, and a weapon upgrade system - that are so simple that it's easy to forget about them altogether. Meanwhile, the level design is incredibly straightforward, making exploration a bore, particularly when it comes to the dead-simple platforming sections. The game's skill tree is even a literal tree. But the real issue with Beast of Reincarnation is that it is full of ideas that already exist elsewhere. The story is like a watered-down version of Nier: Automata 's heartrending postapocalypse, while the boss battles feel ripped out of Monster Hunter (with designs straight from its contemporary Wild Hearts and one specific creature that looks identical to a Stranger Things demodog). Your mobile home base functions much like the one in Death Stranding - you can even shower - and it looks just like an AT-ST from Star Wars . Everywhere you go, there's something from a different game or movie. This is especially disappointing because there is so much potential in Beast of Reincarnation . Not only is the combat thrilling, but, as derivative as it is, the game still manages to create an incredible sense of melancholic moodiness through its sound and visuals. But it never delivers on that; I was excited to learn about the strange religions and customs that were developed by isolated groups of golem, for instance, but the revelations were all surface level and quickly brushed aside. That sums up much of the Beast experience: There are flashes of excitement and intrigue, but mostly you've seen all of this before. At least there's more Pokémon on the way . Beast of Reincarnation launches on August 4th on the PS5, Xbox, and PC. title: China claims global chip leadership thanks to new legal definition of 'integrated circuits'
teaser: China broadened its definition of 'integrated circuit' to cover quantum and photonic chips, boosting IP protection for local tech giants.
summary: China has updated its legal framework by broadening the definition of 'integrated circuit,' replacing specific references to 'semiconductor integrated circuit.' This crucial change, attributed to an expert opinion, aims to bolster intellectual property (IP) protection for advanced chip designs, notably those incorporating photonic and quantum elements. By expanding the scope beyond traditional semiconductor substrates, Beijing seeks to legally shield domestic tech giants—like Alibaba and Huawei—from IP infringement and copying. The move is central to China’s national strategy of building a strong intellectual property nation capable of supporting high-quality technological development.
content: legal China claims global chip leadership thanks to new legal definition of 'integrated circuits' Beijing's new rules also protect against copying local chip designs China has changed its legal definition of semiconductors. The National Intellectual Property Administration yesterday issued an expert opinion on recent changes to the regulations governing intellectual property laws as applied to chips. That document, attributed to Guo He, from the School of Intellectual Property at the Renmin University of China, notes that laws in place around the world define integrated circuits as semiconductors. "Today, photonic integrated devices and quantum chip technology are developing rapidly, and optoelectronic chips are already widely used in some fields," Guo observed, before noting that China's new rules have replaced references to "semiconductor integrated circuit" with "integrated circuit." Beijing made that change to include chips that include photonic and quantum elements. "On the surface, this seems insignificant, as various monolithic integrated circuits worldwide still require semiconductor materials as substrates," Guo wrote, before arguing the significance of the change is that "it demonstrates China's attitude towards intellectual property legislation today: we are no longer conservatives in the intellectual property system." That may be a little boastful, as the most current international agreement covering chip design is the World Intellectual Property Organization's Agreement on Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (TRIP), which describes an integrated circuit as "a product ... in which the elements, at least one of which is an active element, and some or all of the interconnections are integrally formed in and/or on a piece of material and which is intended to perform an electronic function." The Register can imagine that definition extending to optical and quantum elements. The TRIP agreement's provisions on semiconductors also protect the layout of chips - the proprietary arrangement of elements on a silicon die. That's an important protection because it takes plenty of time and money to create a layout, and copying a layout is a chip design shortcut. The main purpose of China's revised Regulation is to strengthen its own layout protection laws, and thanks to its new definition extend them to chips that include optical or quantum elements. Guo says China's chipmakers need extra intellectual property protection, and that the changed Regulation will help to determine patents and settle disputes about the origin of chip designs. The changed laws therefore have "important practical significance for accelerating the construction of a strong intellectual property nation and meeting the needs of high-quality development." That last phrase refers to the Chinese government's policy of developing capabilities in all fields that an advanced nation requires to be globally competitive - including development and manufacturing of semiconductors in all forms. Several Chinese companies - among them Alibaba, Huawei, Cambricon and Loongson - have developed chips that compete strongly with products from US-based rivals. China wants its chipmakers to be strong, so defending them from domestic or foreign copycats makes sense. ®
